strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: extending RL (GRPO-style) training to multi-turn, multi-agent self-play, identifying concrete failure modes (long-horizon credit assignment, heterogeneous role advantage estimation) of naive extensions.

The 'sum-then-normalize' turn-level advantage estimator is a simple but non-trivial fix to a subtle flaw in prior process-supervision GRPO (non-zero-mean advantages), and is theoretically grounded as a GAE special case.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: specialist/generalist training across 3 training + 3 held-out games spanning perfect/imperfect information and cooperative/competitive settings, integration into two distinct MAS frameworks (MAD, AutoGen), and 7 reasoning/QA benchmarks.

Thorough ablations, including self-play vs fixed-opponent (showing overfitting/mode collapse), removal of each algorithmic component, decoupling of algorithm vs. game-selection contributions relative to SPIRAL, direct comparison with concurrent MT-GRPO, scaling to 8B model, and sensitivity analysis of the length-penalty hyperparameter.

Interesting qualitative (reasoning trace) and quantitative (failure-mode taxonomy) analyses that provide some mechanistic insight into why skills transfer from games to MAS (e.g., role-awareness, intent recognition, reduced inter-agent misalignment).
Good reproducibility: detailed prompts, hyperparameters, and reported code/checkpoint release.
weaknesses: The strategic games used (Tic-Tac-Toe, Kuhn Poker, Mini Hanabi and their OOD variants) are toy-scale, two-player only; it is unclear how well the claimed 'multi-agent reasoning' skills would extend to richer N-player or more realistic collaborative/competitive settings, despite the paper's broad framing ('critical step towards more advanced intelligence').

Downstream evaluation of 'generalization to multi-agent systems' ultimately reduces to standard single-turn math/QA benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K, AIME, GPQA, etc.) wrapped in MAD/AutoGen scaffolding; there is no evaluation on tasks that inherently require sustained multi-agent coordination or negotiation, making it hard to assess whether the model is learning genuine multi-agent skills versus better single-turn reasoning that happens to help in these particular MAS wrappers.

Reported absolute gains on MAS benchmarks are often modest (e.g., 3.5% average), and no error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported anywhere, which is concerning given the relatively small training budget (200 steps) and the numerous small benchmark subsets (e.g., AIME24/AMC23 have very few questions).

The reward design (game reward + format reward + length penalty) has several hand-tuned components whose combined and individual effects are not fully disentangled outside of the length-penalty ablation, raising questions about how much of the improvement is attributable to the core algorithmic contribution versus reward engineering.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior work (SPIRAL's RAE for role-conditioning, MT-GRPO's turn-level credit assignment); the paper's contribution is largely a careful recombination and improved ordering of normalization operations rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, though the appendix experiments do help substantiate the empirical value of this specific design choice.

Baselines are limited to SPIRAL and (in the appendix) MT-GRPO; no comparison to other multi-agent RL or credit-assignment methods (e.g., PPO with learned critics, other GAE variants) is provided to contextualize how much of the gain is due to fine-grained credit assignment per se versus the specific self-play/game curriculum.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: extending RL self-play to multi-turn, multi-agent settings covering both cooperative and competitive games, going beyond prior zero-sum-only work (SPIRAL).

The proposed turn-level advantage estimator (sum-then-normalize) is a clean and theoretically motivated fix to a real flaw in the naive GRPO process-supervision baseline (non-zero-mean advantages), and is connected clearly to GAE with gamma=lambda=1.
Agent-specific advantage normalization is a sensible and simple solution to the heterogeneous-role variance problem in multi-agent self-play, and is validated by targeted ablations.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: strategic ability on held-out/OOD games, generalization to two distinct downstream multi-agent frameworks (MAD, AutoGen) on real reasoning benchmarks (AIME, GPQA, MATH, GSM8K, etc.), plus ablations (self-play vs fixed opponent, w/o turn-level, w/o agent-specific).

Interesting qualitative pattern analysis showing that skills learned in games (role awareness, intent recognition/theory-of-mind) transfer in an interpretable way to behavior in downstream multi-agent systems.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, prompts for all game environments, and stated plans to release code/checkpoints.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single base model (Qwen3-4B); there is no evidence the approach transfers to other model families or larger scales, limiting confidence in general applicability.

Games used for training/evaluation are simple two-player, small-action-space environments (Tic-Tac-Toe, Kuhn Poker, Mini Hanabi and their slightly larger counterparts); the N-player and richer-action-space setting is left entirely unexplored, which is acknowledged but substantially narrows the scope of the strategic-ability claims.

No variance/statistical-significance reporting across seeds; single-run numbers are used throughout, which is concerning given some benchmarks (e.g., GPQA-Diamond, AIME) are small and noisy, making some reported gains (e.g., a few percentage points) hard to trust as robust.

The headline percentage improvements quoted in the abstract (10.0% on AIME, 12.5% on GPQA-Diamond) are not clearly traceable to a specific, consistently identified model/table entry, and appear inconsistent with the raw numbers in Table 1 depending on which variant/metric definition is used, reducing clarity and reproducibility of the top-line claims.

The reward function combines game outcome, format regularization, and a length penalty, but there is no ablation isolating the contribution of the auxiliary rewards (especially the length penalty), leaving open whether core gains stem from the proposed advantage-estimation techniques alone or partly from reward shaping.

Baseline comparison is limited to the base model and SPIRAL; no comparison to other plausible multi-agent RL or credit-assignment techniques (e.g., alternative process-reward or hierarchical RL baselines) is provided.

Some ablation results show apparent training collapse/degenerate behavior (e.g., fixed-opponent Kuhn Poker producing -1.000 across metrics, missing Hanabi fixed-opponent rows) without deeper analysis or explanation of why these failures occur.
